questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly distinguishes between a luminous and a non-luminous object?
options: Luminous objects give out light, whereas non-luminous objects do not.
Luminous objects absorb all light, whereas non-luminous objects transmit it.
Luminous objects only reflect light, whereas non-luminous objects give out light.
Luminous objects refract light, whereas non-luminous objects scatter it.

questions.question: What must happen for a person to see an object in a room?
options: Light from the object must be absorbed by the surrounding walls.
Light from the object, either emitted or reflected, must enter the eye.
The eye must project beams of light onto the object to illuminate it.
Light must pass directly through the object without reflecting.

questions.question: How does light enter the eye and where is it detected?
options: It enters through the iris and is detected by the optic nerve at the front.
It enters through the pupil and is detected by the retina at the back surface.
It enters through the cornea and is detected by the pupil.
It enters through the retina and is detected by the pupil at the back.

questions.question: Why can you see a laser beam passing through a dusty room but not in a clean, dust-free room?
options: Dust particles absorb the light beam and make it glow brighter.
Dust particles block the light beam, causing it to slow down and become visible.
The light hits the dust particles and scatters towards your eyes.
The dust particles emit their own light when exposed to the laser.

questions.question: Which statement best describes how an echo is formed?
options: Sound is absorbed by soft surfaces and slowly released back into the room.
Sound reflects from hard surfaces and is heard again after travelling back.
Sound passes through solid walls and speeds up as it exits the other side.
Sound is refracted by the air, causing the pitch to change when it returns.

questions.question: Why do soft materials, like foam or curtains, make good sound absorbers?
options: They reflect sound waves in many regular directions to cancel them out.
Sound waves transfer energy to them by making the particles in the soft materials vibrate.
They prevent particles from moving, keeping the sound trapped.
They increase the frequency of the sound waves until they can no longer be heard.

questions.question: In light diagrams, what is the 'normal' line?
options: A line drawn parallel to the mirror's surface.
An imaginary line drawn at 90 degrees to the point of reflection.
The path that the reflected ray of light takes.
A line representing the boundary between two different materials.

questions.question: How are the angles of incidence and reflection measured?
options: Along the surface of the mirror from the incoming and outgoing rays.
Between the incoming ray and the reflected ray directly.
From the normal to the respective incident and reflected rays.
From the light source to the eye.

questions.question: A ray of light hits a flat mirror with an angle of incidence of 35 degrees to the normal. What is the angle of reflection?
options: 35 degrees, on the other side of the normal.
55 degrees, on the same side of the normal.
90 degrees, along the normal line.
145 degrees, on the other side of the normal.

questions.question: If a toy is placed 20 cm in front of a flat mirror, where does its reflection appear to be?
options: 10 cm behind the mirror, directly opposite the toy.
20 cm behind the mirror, directly opposite the toy.
40 cm behind the mirror, shifted to the side.
Right on the surface of the mirror.

questions.question: When you look at your image in a flat mirror, how does it compare to you?
options: It is upside down and flipped left-to-right.
It is the right way up and exactly identical with no changes.
It is the right way up but is laterally inverted (left and right are swapped).
It is upside down but otherwise has the same orientation.

questions.question: How do transparent and opaque objects differ in how they affect light?
options: Transparent objects reflect all light, while opaque objects transmit it.
Transparent objects transmit light through them, while opaque objects do not.
Transparent objects scatter light, while opaque objects let it pass cleanly.
Transparent objects absorb all light, while opaque objects reflect it.

questions.question: What is a shadow and how is it formed?
options: An area where light bends around an object to form a dark pattern.
A region where reflected light from a mirror is focused.
An unlit area in the shape of an object that is blocking light.
A glowing area created behind an object when it absorbs energy.

questions.question: What is amplitude, and how does it affect how we hear a sound?
options: It is the speed of the wave, and a higher amplitude makes the pitch higher.
It is the distance or size of a vibration, and a greater amplitude makes the sound louder.
It is the number of vibrations per second, and a lower amplitude makes the sound quieter.
It is the wavelength of a sound wave, and a greater amplitude makes the pitch lower.

questions.question: If the frequency of a sound wave is increased, what change will you hear in the sound?
options: The sound will become louder.
The sound will have a higher pitch.
The sound will become quieter.
The sound will have a lower pitch.

questions.question: Why does sound travel fastest through solids compared to liquids or gases?
options: Solids have no particles, which allows sound waves to travel without any resistance.
The particles in solids are very far apart, so they have more room to vibrate.
Solids have strong attractive forces between particles, causing many to vibrate when one does.
Solids are colder than liquids and gases, which increases the speed of vibrations.

questions.question: Why can sound not travel through a vacuum, such as outer space?
options: Because a vacuum is too cold for sound waves to survive.
Because sound waves require particles to vibrate, and there are no particles in a vacuum.
Because light waves in a vacuum block sound waves from moving.
Because gravity is too weak in a vacuum to pull the sound waves forward.

questions.question: When a sound wave travels through the air from a speaker to your ear, what actually moves?
options: Air particles travel all the way from the speaker into your ear.
A pattern of vibrating particles creates a sound wave, but individual air particles do not travel with the wave.
Heat energy travels through the air without affecting the particles.
Light rays carry the sound particles through the air.
